title: Unitary-invariant norms and symmetric gauges
subtitle: G2 lecture 058000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Standalone slide treatment of the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix; authored derivations, worked calculations and local SVG diagrams.

slides.title: Which measurements survive a change of basis?
slides.lead: The same linear map can have different matrix entries in different orthonormal bases.
body: If U and V are unitary matrices on the output and input spaces, respectively, a coordinate change replaces A by UAV*. A unitarily invariant norm assigns the same size to both matrices.
This invariance is the natural requirement for geometry: the measurement should depend on the map rather than on the arbitrary frames used to write it.
slides.takeaway: Unitary invariance removes dependence on orthonormal coordinate choices.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 058000 · Which measurements survive a change of basis?

slides.title: SVD reduces the problem to a vector gauge
slides.lead: For a fixed m-by-n shape, the SVD writes A as unitary factors around a rectangular diagonal matrix of singular values.
body: If the norm is unitarily invariant, its value on A equals its value on that singular-value diagonal. Therefore it is determined by a function of the nonnegative singular-value list.
Permuting diagonal singular values or changing individual signs can be implemented by unitary matrices. The corresponding list function must have permutation and sign symmetry.
slides.takeaway: An invariant matrix norm is encoded by a symmetric gauge of singular values.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 058000 · SVD reduces the problem to a vector gauge

slides.title: What is a symmetric gauge?
slides.lead: A symmetric gauge is a norm on a coordinate list that is unchanged by permutations and coordinatewise sign changes.
body: The usual ℓ₁, ℓ₂, and ℓ∞ norms are symmetric gauges. Their corresponding matrix measurements are nuclear, Frobenius, and operator norms.
For a fixed matrix shape, every such gauge defines a unitarily invariant matrix norm when applied to the singular values. The triangle inequality follows by weak majorization for sums.
slides.takeaway: Permutation and sign invariance are the defining symmetries of singular-value gauges.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 058000 · What is a symmetric gauge?

slides.title: One matrix, several gauges
slides.lead: Take a diagonal matrix with singular values (4,2,1).
body: The operator norm gives four, the nuclear norm gives seven, and the Frobenius norm gives √(16+4+1)=√21. All three are unitarily invariant; each emphasizes a different aspect of the singular-value profile.
A Ky Fan 2 norm gives 4+2=6. The family of symmetric gauges contains many more measurements than the three familiar Schatten endpoints.
slides.takeaway: The gauge determines what kind of singular-value information the norm aggregates.

slides.title: Why the gauge construction satisfies the triangle inequality
slides.lead: A singular-value sum obeys weak majorization, even when each singular value does not obey a separate triangle inequality.
body: Apply σ(A+B)≺_w σ(A)+σ(B), then use the symmetric gauge’s monotonicity under weak majorization. The final step is the ordinary triangle inequality for the gauge on lists.
This proof avoids trying to align the singular vectors of A and B, which in general belong to different directions.
slides.takeaway: Weak majorization is the bridge from list norms to matrix triangle inequalities.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 058000 · Why the gauge construction satisfies the triangle inequality

slides.title: One comparison controls every invariant gauge
slides.lead: Suppose σ(A) is weakly majorized by σ(B).
body: Every symmetric gauge is convex, sign invariant, and permutation invariant, so majorization descent proves φ(σ(A))≤φ(σ(B)). Consequently every unitarily invariant norm of the same matrix shape gives A no larger a value than B.
This is why Ky Fan domination is often a more informative theorem than a bound for any single norm.
slides.takeaway: Ky Fan prefix inequalities imply the complete family of fixed-shape invariant norm inequalities.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 058000 · One comparison controls every invariant gauge

slides.title: An operator ideal asks for more
slides.lead: Being invariant for a single matrix shape does not guarantee a coherent norm across many spaces and dimensions.
body: In operator-ideal theory the class of admissible operators and its norm must be stable under left and right composition by bounded maps. Standard estimates compare the ideal norm of LAR to the operator norms of L and R.
This additional compatibility is important for rectangular subspace residuals, restrictions, and infinite-dimensional problems.
slides.takeaway: Operator ideals combine unitary symmetry with composition stability.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 058000 · An operator ideal asks for more

slides.title: What an invariant norm can and cannot compare
slides.lead: Fixing a matrix shape makes left-right unitary invariance a straightforward condition.
body: Comparing an m-by-n matrix with a larger matrix obtained by zero padding requires more than choosing arbitrary invariant norms independently on each shape.

Compatible families such as the Schatten norms respect zero padding. The next lecture makes this extra rectangular compatibility explicit and shows why it cannot be inferred from fixed-shape invariance alone.
slides.takeaway: Invariant gauges on separate shapes need a compatibility rule before comparing dimensions.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 058000 · What an invariant norm can and cannot compare

slides.title: Why the distinction matters in perturbation estimates
slides.lead: Spectral-subspace perturbations often involve different source and target subspaces.
body: A rectangular residual can be represented in several orthonormal frames. Its norm should be unchanged by those frame choices, and ideally unchanged by isometric embedding into a larger ambient Hilbert space.
The first demand is fixed-shape unitary invariance; the second asks for a coherent cross-space norm family. Keeping them separate prevents a missing hypothesis in later operator inequalities.
slides.takeaway: Declare both coordinate invariance and any cross-dimensional compatibility required.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 058000 · Why the distinction matters in perturbation estimates

slides.title: Reconstruct the two directions
slides.lead: An invariant matrix norm corresponds to a symmetric gauge, and a symmetric gauge constructs an invariant matrix norm.
body: For the first direction, diagonalize by SVD and inspect permutation and sign matrices. For the second, define φ(σ(A)) and derive its triangle inequality through weak majorization.
Then state which extra ideal and padding hypotheses are needed when matrix shapes or underlying spaces change.
slides.takeaway: SVD, weak majorization, and compatibility assumptions finish the classification.
